Section context: Worked twice: once for a free function and once inside `fit` for an estimator class.
Notes: Trigger: deprecating a parameter. Names the exact warning class.

Original text: When the change is in a class, we validate and raise warning in ``fit``::
Atomic rule: Validate a deprecated parameter and raise its warning in fit, not in __init__.
Section context: Matches the constructor rule on develop.html: 'There should be no logic, not even input validation' in __init__.
Notes: Trigger: deprecating a parameter of an estimator class.

Original text:
As in these examples, the warning message should always give both the
version in which the deprecation happened and the version in which the
old behavior will be removed.
Atomic rule: Name both the deprecation version and the removal version in the warning message.
Section context: 'so that users will have enough time to adapt their code to the new behaviour'. The same sentence is repeated in the Change-the-default section as 'Similar to deprecations, the warning message should always give both the version in which the change happened and the version in which the old behavior will be removed.'
Notes: Trigger: deprecations. Two version strings must appear in the message.

Original text:
If the deprecation happened in version
0.x-dev, the message should say deprecation occurred in version 0.x and
the removal will be in 0.(x+2).
Atomic rule: Quote the release version, not the dev version, and set removal two releases later.
Section context: 'For example, if the deprecation happened in version 0.18-dev, the message should say it happened in version 0.18 and the old behavior will be removed in version 0.20.'
Notes: Trigger: deprecations. An arithmetic relation between two version strings.

Original text:
The warning message should also include a brief explanation of the change and point
users to an alternative.
Atomic rule: Explain the change briefly in the warning and point users to an alternative.
Section context: Follows the two-versions requirement; 'brief' is not defined and the worked messages vary in length.
Notes: Trigger: deprecations.

Original text:
In addition, a deprecation note should be added in the docstring, recalling the
same information as the deprecation warning as explained above. Use the
``.. deprecated::`` directive:
Atomic rule: Add a .. deprecated:: note to the docstring repeating the warning's information.
Section context: Worked as '.. deprecated:: 0.13 / ``k`` was renamed to ``n_clusters`` in version 0.13 and will be removed in 0.15.'
Notes: Trigger: deprecations. Names the exact directive.

Original text:
What's more, a deprecation requires a test which ensures that the warning is
raised in relevant cases but not in other cases.
Atomic rule: Add a test asserting the deprecation warning is raised only in the relevant cases.
Section context: The same requirement is repeated for default-value changes: 'Finally, we need a test which ensures that the warning is raised in relevant cases but not in other cases.'
Notes: Trigger: deprecations.

Original text:
The warning should be caught
in all other tests (using e.g., ``@pytest.mark.filterwarnings``),
Atomic rule: Catch the deprecation warning in every other test, e.g. with @pytest.mark.filterwarnings.
Section context: Repeated verbatim in the Change-the-default section. The Tips page notes 'our continuous integration tests will error if ``FutureWarning`` isn't properly caught'.
Notes: Trigger: deprecations. Names the decorator to use.

Original text: and there should be no warning in the examples.
Atomic rule: Leave the gallery examples free of the deprecation warning.
Section context: `SKLEARN_WARNINGS_AS_ERRORS=1` in the documentation build 'is checking that the documentation build, in particular running examples, does not produce any warnings'.
Notes: Trigger: deprecations. Repeated verbatim in the Change-the-default section.

Source: https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html | Maintaining backwards compatibility > Change the default value of a parameter
Original text:
If the default value of a parameter needs to be changed, please replace the
default value with a specific value (e.g., ``"warn"``) and raise
``FutureWarning`` when users are using the default value.
Atomic rule: Replace a changing default with a sentinel value and raise FutureWarning when it is left in place.
Section context: Worked twice, for a free function and for a class where the check happens in `fit`; the example uses the sentinel string "warn".
Notes: Trigger: changing a parameter's default value.

Source: https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html | Maintaining backwards compatibility > Change the default value of a parameter
Original text:
Similar to deprecations, the warning message should always give both the
version in which the change happened and the version in which the old behavior
will be removed.
Atomic rule: Name both the change version and the removal version in a default-change warning.
Section context: Explicitly derived from the deprecation section, which states the identical requirement for deprecation warnings.
Notes: Trigger: changing a default. Same obligation as the deprecation warning rule.

Source: https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html | Maintaining backwards compatibility > Change the default value of a parameter
Original text:
The parameter description in the docstring needs to be updated accordingly by adding
a ``versionchanged`` directive with the old and new default value, pointing to the
version when the change will be effective:
Atomic rule: Add a .. versionchanged:: directive to the parameter docstring giving the old and new defaults.
Section context: Worked as '.. versionchanged:: 0.22 / The default value for `n_clusters` will change from 5 to 10 in version 0.22.'
Notes: Trigger: changing a default. Names the exact directive and its required content.

Source: https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html | Maintaining backwards compatibility > Change the default value of a parameter
Original text:
Finally, we need a test which ensures that the warning is raised in relevant cases but
not in other cases.
Atomic rule: Add a test asserting the default-change warning is raised only in the relevant cases.
Section context: Word-for-word the deprecation section's test requirement, applied to the default-change warning.
Notes: Trigger: changing a default.

Source: https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html | Maintaining backwards compatibility > Change the default value of a parameter
Original text:
The warning should be caught in all other tests
(using e.g., ``@pytest.mark.filterwarnings``), and there should be no warning
in the examples.
Atomic rule: Catch the default-change warning in all other tests and keep it out of the examples.
Section context: Repeats the deprecation section's two sentences as one, for the default-change warning.
Notes: Trigger: changing a default.

Original text:
Configure `git blame` to ignore the commit that migrated the code style to
  `black` and then `ruff`.

  .. prompt:: bash

      git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs
Atomic rule: Point git blame at .git-blame-ignore-revs in your local clone.
Section context: 'Find out more information in black's documentation for avoiding ruining git blame.' The rest of the section is reading advice with no obligations.
Notes: Changes local git config, which no artifact of a contribution records.

Original text:
It should not, however, take
the actual training data as an argument, as this is left to the ``fit()`` method::
Atomic rule: Do not accept training data as an argument to an estimator's __init__.
Section context: The counter-example is labelled in the code block: ``clf3 = SGDClassifier([[1, 2], [2, 3]], [-1, 1]) # WRONG!``
Notes: Trigger: adding or changing an estimator class.

Original text:
Ideally, the arguments accepted by ``__init__`` should all be keyword arguments with a
default value. In other words, a user should be able to instantiate an estimator without
passing any arguments to it.
Atomic rule: Give every __init__ argument a default value so the estimator can be constructed with no arguments.
Section context: 'In some cases, where there are no sane defaults for an argument, they can be left without a default value. In scikit-learn itself, we have very few places, only in some meta-estimators, where the sub-estimator(s) argument is a required argument.'
Notes: Trigger: adding or changing an estimator class.

Original text:
These initial
arguments (or parameters) are always remembered by the estimator. Also note that they
should not be documented under the "Attributes" section, but rather under the
"Parameters" section for that estimator.
Atomic rule: Document constructor arguments under Parameters, not under Attributes.
Section context: The Estimated Attributes section states the complement: trailing-underscore attributes are documented as 'Attributes' and leading-underscore ones are not documented.
Notes: Trigger: estimator docstrings. Two named docstring sections.

Original text:
In addition, **every keyword argument accepted by** ``__init__`` **should
correspond to an attribute on the instance**.
Atomic rule: Set an instance attribute for every keyword argument __init__ accepts.
Section context: 'Scikit-learn relies on this to find the relevant attributes to set on an estimator when doing model selection.' The summary block shows `self.param1 = param1`.
Notes: Trigger: estimator constructors. Enforced at runtime by get_params/set_params.

Original text:
# WRONG: the object's attributes should have exactly the name of
        # the argument in the constructor
        self.param3 = param2
Atomic rule: Give the stored attribute exactly the name of the constructor argument.
Section context: Comment inside the block of wrong code, immediately below the rule that every keyword argument should correspond to an attribute.
Notes: Names the exact correspondence the preceding rule leaves implicit.

Original text:
There should be no logic, not even input validation, and the parameters should not be
changed; which also means ideally they should not be mutable objects such as lists or
dictionaries.
Atomic rule: Put no logic and no input validation in an estimator's __init__.
Section context: 'The reason for postponing the validation is that if ``__init__`` includes input validation, then the same validation would have to be performed in ``set_params``, which is used in algorithms like GridSearchCV.'
Notes: Trigger: estimator constructors. The mutable-object half is hedged with 'ideally'.

Original text:
If they're mutable, they should be copied before being modified. The
corresponding logic should be put where the parameters are used, typically in ``fit``.
Atomic rule: Copy a mutable constructor argument before modifying it, and do so where it is used.
Section context: The Cloning section repeats it: 'As already mentioned that when constructor arguments are mutable, they should be copied before modifying them.'
Notes: Trigger: estimators taking mutable parameters.

Original text:
Also it is expected that parameters with trailing ``_`` are **not to be set
inside the** ``__init__`` **method**.
Atomic rule: Do not set trailing-underscore attributes inside __init__.
Section context: 'More details on attributes that are not init arguments come shortly' - the Estimated Attributes section reserves the trailing underscore for values learned in fit.
Notes: Trigger: estimator constructors. A name-shape prohibition, readable statically.

Original text:
The number of samples, i.e. ``X.shape[0]`` should be the same as ``y.shape[0]``. If this
requirement is not met, an exception of type ``ValueError`` should be raised.
Atomic rule: Raise ValueError when X and y have different numbers of samples.
Section context: `validate_data` and `check_X_y` are offered elsewhere as the helpers that do this; the exception type is named exactly.
Notes: Trigger: estimator fit methods.

Original text:
However, to
make it possible to use the estimator as part of a pipeline that can
mix both supervised and unsupervised transformers, even unsupervised
estimators need to accept a ``y=None`` keyword argument in
the second position that is just ignored by the estimator.
Atomic rule: Accept an ignored y=None keyword in second position on an unsupervised estimator's fit.
Section context: Stated with its reason, pipeline compatibility. The Estimator types section restates it for clustering algorithms as 'Ideally, they should accept a ``y`` parameter in their ``fit`` method, but it should be ignored.'
Notes: Trigger: unsupervised estimators. An exact signature position.

Original text:
For the same reason, ``fit_predict``, ``fit_transform``, ``score``
and ``partial_fit`` methods need to accept a ``y`` argument in
the second place if they are implemented.
Atomic rule: Accept y in second position on fit_predict, fit_transform, score and partial_fit.
Section context: Extends the fit signature rule to a closed list of four methods, conditioned on them being implemented.
Notes: Trigger: only the listed methods, and only where the estimator implements them.

Original text:
The method should return the object (``self``). This pattern is useful
to be able to implement quick one liners in an IPython session such as::
Atomic rule: Return self from fit.
Section context: Worked as `y_predicted = SGDClassifier(alpha=10).fit(X_train, y_train).predict(X_test)`; chaining breaks without it.
Notes: Trigger: estimator fit methods. One satisfying return value.

Original text:
However, any parameter that can have a value assigned prior to
having access to the data should be an ``__init__`` keyword argument.
Atomic rule: Take any parameter that can be set before seeing the data as an __init__ keyword argument.
Section context: Immediately followed by the same rule from the other side: 'Ideally, **fit parameters should be restricted to directly data dependent variables**.'
Notes: Trigger: estimator signatures. Worked with the tol counter-example.

Original text:
Ideally, **fit
parameters should be restricted to directly data dependent variables**. For instance a
Gram matrix or an affinity matrix which are precomputed from the data matrix ``X`` are
data dependent. A tolerance stopping criterion ``tol`` is not directly data dependent
Atomic rule: Restrict fit parameters to directly data-dependent variables.
Section context: 'Ideally' hedges a rule the preceding sentence states unhedged: 'any parameter that can have a value assigned prior to having access to the data should be an ``__init__`` keyword argument'.
Notes: Same split of parameters between __init__ and fit, stated from the fit side and hedged.

Original text:
When ``fit`` is called, any previous call to ``fit`` should be ignored. In
general, calling ``estimator.fit(X1)`` and then ``estimator.fit(X2)`` should
be the same as only calling ``estimator.fit(X2)``.
Atomic rule: Make a second call to fit discard the state left by the first.
Section context: 'However, this may not be true in practice when ``fit`` depends on some random process' and '``warm_start=True`` means that the previous state of the trainable parameters of the estimator are reused' - two exceptions granted in the same paragraph.
Notes: Trigger: estimator fit methods.

Original text:
attributes which you'd want to expose to your
users as public attributes and have been estimated or learned from the data must always
have a name ending with trailing underscore, for example the coefficients of some
regression estimator would be stored in a ``coef_`` attribute after ``fit`` has been
called.
Atomic rule: Name every public learned attribute with a trailing underscore.
Section context: 'must always' - and `check_is_fitted` keys off exactly this convention: 'By default check_is_fitted checks if there are any attributes in the instance with a trailing underscore'.
Notes: Trigger: estimators storing learned values.

Original text:
Similarly, attributes that you learn in the process and you'd like to store yet
not expose to the user, should have a leading underscore, e.g. ``_intermediate_coefs``.
Atomic rule: Name a learned but non-public attribute with a leading underscore.
Section context: Paired with the trailing-underscore rule for public learned attributes; the following sentence ties each group to a documentation obligation.
Notes: Trigger: estimators storing internal learned values.

Original text:
You'd need to document the first group (with a trailing underscore) as "Attributes" and
no need to document the second group (with a leading underscore).
Atomic rule: Document trailing-underscore attributes in the docstring's Attributes section.
Section context: Complements the Instantiation rule that constructor arguments belong under Parameters, not Attributes.
Notes: Trigger: estimators with learned public attributes.

Original text:
The estimated attributes are expected to be overridden when you call ``fit`` a second
time.
Atomic rule: Overwrite the estimated attributes on a second call to fit.
Section context: Restates the Fitting section's rule that a second fit must behave as if the first had not happened, at the level of the stored attributes.
Notes: Trigger: estimator fit methods.

Original text:
Estimators that expect tabular input should set a `n_features_in_`
attribute at `fit` time to indicate the number of features that the estimator
expects for subsequent calls to :term:`predict` or :term:`transform`.
Atomic rule: Set n_features_in_ at fit time on an estimator that expects tabular input.
Section context: 'See `SLEP010` for details.' and 'Using :func:`~sklearn.utils.validation.validate_data` would automatically set these attributes for you.'
Notes: Trigger: estimators taking tabular input. An exact attribute name.

Original text:
Similarly, if estimators are given dataframes such as pandas or polars, they should
set a ``feature_names_in_`` attribute to indicate the features names of the input data,
detailed in `SLEP007
Atomic rule: Set feature_names_in_ when the estimator is fitted on a dataframe.
Section context: Same paragraph as n_features_in_, and `validate_data` sets both automatically.
Notes: Trigger: estimators accepting dataframes. An exact attribute name.

Original text:
You can check whether your estimator
adheres to the scikit-learn interface and standards by running
:func:`~sklearn.utils.estimator_checks.check_estimator` on an instance.
Atomic rule: Run check_estimator on a new estimator instance.
Section context: 'The :func:`~sklearn.utils.estimator_checks.parametrize_with_checks` pytest decorator can also be used'. contributing.html offers the same suite as `pytest sklearn/tests/test_common.py -k <Estimator>`.
Notes: Trigger: new or changed estimators. Two ways of invoking the same check suite.

Original text:
Out of all the methods that an estimator implements, ``fit`` is usually the one you
want to implement yourself. Other methods such as ``set_params``, ``get_params``, etc.
are implemented in :class:`~sklearn.base.BaseEstimator`, which you should inherit from.
Atomic rule: Inherit a new estimator from BaseEstimator.
Section context: 'if you don't inherit from the right mixins, either there will be a large amount of boilerplate code for you to implement and keep in sync with scikit-learn development, or your estimator might not function the same way as a scikit-learn estimator.'
Notes: Trigger: new estimator classes.

Original text:
It is particularly important to notice that mixins should be "on the left" while
    the ``BaseEstimator`` should be "on the right" in the inheritance list for proper
    MRO.
Atomic rule: List mixins before BaseEstimator in a new estimator's bases.
Section context: Its consequence is stated: proper method resolution order. The worked example is `class TemplateClassifier(ClassifierMixin, BaseEstimator)`.
Notes: Trigger: new estimator classes. An exact ordering, readable from the class statement.

Original text:
Estimators can customize the behavior of :func:`base.clone` by overriding the
:func:`base.BaseEstimator.__sklearn_clone__` method. `__sklearn_clone__` must return an
instance of the estimator.
Atomic rule: Return an estimator instance from __sklearn_clone__.
Section context: '`__sklearn_clone__` is useful when an estimator needs to hold on to some state when :func:`base.clone` is called on the estimator. For example, FrozenEstimator makes use of this.'
Notes: Trigger: only where the contribution overrides __sklearn_clone__.

Original text:
**Transformers** inherit from :class:`~base.TransformerMixin`, and implement a `transform`
method.
Atomic rule: Make a transformer inherit TransformerMixin and implement transform.
Section context: One of four estimator kinds, each tied to its mixin; the set_output API 'is automatically defined if the transformer defines get_feature_names_out and subclasses TransformerMixin'.
Notes: Trigger: adding a transformer.

Original text:
Note
that they should never change the number of input samples, and the output of `transform`
should correspond to its input samples in the same given order.
Atomic rule: Keep transform's output aligned one-to-one and in order with its input samples.
Section context: Sharpens the page's own definition of a Transformer, 'e.g. by adding, changing, or removing columns, but not by adding or removing rows'.
Notes: Trigger: transformers.

Original text:
**Regressors** inherit from :class:`~base.RegressorMixin`, and implement a `predict` method.
They should accept numerical ``y`` in their `fit` method.
Atomic rule: Make a regressor inherit RegressorMixin, implement predict and accept numerical y.
Section context: 'Regressors use :func:`~metrics.r2_score` by default in their score method' - inheriting the mixin is what supplies score.
Notes: Trigger: adding a regressor.

Original text:
**Classifiers** inherit from :class:`~base.ClassifierMixin`. If it applies, classifiers can
implement ``decision_function`` to return raw decision values, based on which
``predict`` can make its decision.
Atomic rule: Make a classifier inherit ClassifierMixin.
Section context: 'If calculating probabilities is supported, classifiers can also implement ``predict_proba`` and ``predict_log_proba``' - those two are optional, the mixin is not.
Notes: Trigger: adding a classifier.

Original text:
Classifiers should accept ``y`` (target) arguments to ``fit`` that are sequences (lists,
arrays) of either strings or integers.
Atomic rule: Accept string or integer label sequences as y in a classifier's fit.
Section context: The following sentences forbid assuming a contiguous integer range and require `classes_`, with `self.classes_, y = np.unique(y, return_inverse=True)` given as the easiest way.
Notes: Trigger: classifiers.

Original text:
They should not assume that the class labels are
a contiguous range of integers; instead, they should store a list of classes in a
``classes_`` attribute or property.
Atomic rule: Store the observed labels in classes_ instead of assuming a contiguous integer range.
Section context: Worked with `self.classes_, y = np.unique(y, return_inverse=True)`; the trailing underscore also makes it an estimated attribute under the Estimated Attributes rules.
Notes: Trigger: classifiers. Names the exact attribute.

Original text:
The order of class labels in this attribute should
match the order in which ``predict_proba``, ``predict_log_proba`` and
``decision_function`` return their values.
Atomic rule: Order classes_ to match the column order of predict_proba, predict_log_proba and decision_function.
Section context: Followed by the predict recipe `return self.classes_[np.argmax(D, axis=1)]`, which is only correct if the orders agree.
Notes: Trigger: classifiers implementing any of the three methods.

Original text:
A classifier's ``predict`` method should return arrays containing class labels from
``classes_``.
Atomic rule: Return labels drawn from classes_ out of a classifier's predict.
Section context: 'In a classifier that implements ``decision_function``, this can be achieved with: `return self.classes_[np.argmax(D, axis=1)]`'.
Notes: Trigger: classifiers.

Original text: **Clustering algorithms** inherit from :class:`~base.ClusterMixin`.
Atomic rule: Make a clustering algorithm inherit ClusterMixin.
Section context: Fourth of the four estimator kinds, each tied to its mixin.
Notes: Trigger: adding a clustering algorithm.

Original text:
Ideally, they should
accept a ``y`` parameter in their ``fit`` method, but it should be ignored.
Atomic rule: Accept and ignore a y parameter in a clustering algorithm's fit.
Section context: 'Ideally'. The Fitting section states the same requirement unhedged for every unsupervised estimator: 'even unsupervised estimators need to accept a ``y=None`` keyword argument in the second position that is just ignored'.
Notes: Clustering-specific restatement of the unsupervised fit signature rule, hedged.

Original text:
Clustering
algorithms should set a ``labels_`` attribute, storing the labels assigned to each
sample.
Atomic rule: Set a labels_ attribute holding the per-sample cluster assignment.
Section context: 'If applicable, they can also implement a ``predict`` method, returning the labels assigned to newly given samples' - predict is optional, labels_ is not.
Notes: Trigger: clustering algorithms. An exact attribute name.

Original text:
You can change the default values by defining a `__sklearn_tags__()` method
which returns the new values for your estimator's tags.
Atomic rule: Override __sklearn_tags__ to change an estimator's default tags.
Section context: 'It is unlikely that the default values for each tag will suit the needs of your specific estimator.' The worked example calls `super().__sklearn_tags__()` first.
Notes: Trigger: only where the contribution needs non-default tags.

Original text:
You can create a new subclass of :class:`~sklearn.utils.Tags` if you wish to add new
tags to the existing set. Note that all attributes that you add in a child class need
to have a default value.
Atomic rule: Give every attribute added to a Tags subclass a default value.
Section context: Worked with a `@dataclass class MyTags(Tags): my_tag: bool = True`; the dataclass machinery is what makes the default mandatory.
Notes: Trigger: only where the contribution subclasses Tags.

Original text:
You can opt-out of the `set_output` API by setting `auto_wrap_output_keys=None`
when defining a custom subclass::
Atomic rule: Opt a transformer out of set_output with auto_wrap_output_keys=None.
Section context: 'The default value for `auto_wrap_output_keys` is `("transform",)`, which automatically wraps `fit_transform` and `transform`.'
Notes: Trigger: only where the contribution opts a transformer out of set_output.

Original text:
Super classes' `__init_subclass__` should
**not** depend on `auto_wrap_output_keys`.
Atomic rule: Do not let a super class's __init_subclass__ depend on auto_wrap_output_keys.
Section context: 'The `TransformerMixin` uses the `__init_subclass__` mechanism to consume `auto_wrap_output_keys` and pass all other keyword arguments to its super class' - the keyword is consumed before the super class sees it.
Notes: Trigger: transformers defining __init_subclass__.

Original text:
An estimator can change the behavior by implementing a `__sklearn_is_fitted__`
method taking no input and returning a boolean. If this method exists,
:func:`~sklearn.utils.validation.check_is_fitted` simply returns its output.
Atomic rule: Give __sklearn_is_fitted__ no parameters and a boolean return.
Section context: 'By default check_is_fitted checks if there are any attributes in the instance with a trailing underscore' - this method replaces that check entirely.
Notes: Trigger: only where the contribution implements __sklearn_is_fitted__.

Original text:
To customize the URL linking to an estimator's documentation (i.e. when clicking on the
"?" icon), override the `_doc_link_module` and `_doc_link_template` attributes.
Atomic rule: Override _doc_link_module and _doc_link_template to customize an estimator's doc link.
Section context: '.. warning:: The HTML representation API is experimental and the API is subject to change.'
Notes: Trigger: only where the contribution customizes the HTML repr doc link.

Original text:
Set
`_doc_link_module` to the name of the (top level) module that contains your estimator.
If the value does not match the top level module name, the HTML representation will not
contain a link to the documentation.
Atomic rule: Set _doc_link_module to the top-level module name containing the estimator.
Section context: The consequence of getting it wrong is stated, and the scikit-learn value is given: 'For scikit-learn estimators this is set to `"sklearn"`.'
Notes: Trigger: estimators customizing the HTML repr doc link.

Original text:
If you need more variables you
should implement the `_doc_link_url_param_generator` method which should return a
dictionary of the variables and their values.
Atomic rule: Return a dict of template variables from _doc_link_url_param_generator.
Section context: 'By default, it can contain two variables: `estimator_module` ... and `estimator_name`' - the method is only needed beyond those two.
Notes: Trigger: doc-link templates needing variables beyond the two defaults.

Original text:
The
scikit-learn project tries to closely follow the official Python guidelines
detailed in `PEP8 <https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0008>`_ that
detail how code should be formatted and indented. Please read it and
follow it.
Atomic rule: Format contributed Python code according to PEP8.
Section context: The section opens 'Of course, there are special cases and there will be exceptions to these rules' and closes 'we expect that enforcing those constraints on all new contributions will get the overall code base quality in the right direction.' ruff enforces the mechanical part: `[tool.ruff] line-length = 88` and `extend-select = ["E501", "W", "I", ...]`, run with `--fix` in .pre-commit-config.yaml.
Notes: Pointer to an external standard; traversal stops at PEP8.

Original text:
Use underscores to separate words in non class names: ``n_samples``
  rather than ``nsamples``.
Atomic rule: Separate words with underscores in non-class names.
Section context: The section opens 'Of course, there are special cases and there will be exceptions to these rules' and closes 'we expect that enforcing those constraints on all new contributions will get the overall code base quality in the right direction.' The rule is given with a worked pair, n_samples rather than nsamples.
Notes: First of the eight added guidelines.

Original text:
Avoid multiple statements on one line. Prefer a line return after
  a control flow statement (``if``/``for``).
Atomic rule: Put no more than one statement on a line, and break after if and for.
Section context: The section opens 'Of course, there are special cases and there will be exceptions to these rules' and closes 'we expect that enforcing those constraints on all new contributions will get the overall code base quality in the right direction.' ruff's E-rules cover multiple statements on one line, and ruff-format rewrites them.
Notes: Names the exact constructs it governs.

Original text: Use absolute imports
Atomic rule: Use absolute imports.
Section context: The section opens 'Of course, there are special cases and there will be exceptions to these rules' and closes 'we expect that enforcing those constraints on all new contributions will get the overall code base quality in the right direction.' pyproject.toml sets `[tool.ruff.lint.flake8-tidy-imports] ban-relative-imports = "all"`, and cython-lint runs with `--ban-relative-imports`.
Notes: Three words, no exception offered anywhere on the page.

Original text:
Unit tests should use imports exactly as client code would.
  If ``sklearn.foo`` exports a class or function that is implemented in
  ``sklearn.foo.bar.baz``, the test should import it from ``sklearn.foo``.

In other cases, be sure to call :func:`check_array` on any array-like argument

the routine should accept a keyword

Original text:
The `Display` class should define one or both class methods: `from_estimator` and

`__init__` method contains only the data needed to create the visualization.

After these
class methods create the display object with the computed values, then call the

Notes: Trigger: Display class methods.

consistent with the number of axes it expects and then draws on those axes.

In this case, we suggest using matplotlib's
`~matplotlib.gridspec.GridSpecFromSubplotSpec` to split up the space::
Atomic rule: Subdivide a single passed axes with GridSpecFromSubplotSpec.

Original text:
Therefore, it is also not imported globally in the display classes, but only
within the plotting functions where it is actually needed.
Atomic rule: Import matplotlib inside the plotting function, never at module level.
Section context: 'To keep `scikit-learn` as lightweight as possible, `matplotlib` is not a required dependency for building and using the package (it is only required for building the docs).'

Before importing it, use
`check_matplotlib_support` from `_optional_dependencies.py
Atomic rule: Call check_matplotlib_support before importing matplotlib.

For testing, use the `pyplot` fixture from `conftest.py

Avoid memoryview slicing: memoryview slicing might be costly or misleading in some cases and

Section context: 'even if handling fewer dimensions in some context would be preferable' - the section closes off the obvious reason to deviate.

Original text: Decorate final classes or methods with ``@final`` (this allows removing virtual tables when needed)
Atomic rule: Decorate final Cython classes and methods with @final.

Notes: Trigger: Cython classes and methods that are not subclassed.

Original text: Inline methods and functions when it makes sense
Atomic rule: Inline Cython methods and functions where it helps.
Section context: 'when it makes sense', in a list that ends 'In doubt, read the generated C or C++ code if you can'.
Notes: Trigger: Cython code.

Interactions with the CPython interpreter must be avoided as much as possible in

Atomic rule: Release the GIL explicitly with prange(nogil=True) or a with nogil block.
Section context: Worked with `cdef inline void my_func(self) nogil:` containing a `with nogil:` block; declaring nogil alone is stated to do nothing.
Notes: Trigger: Cython code declaring nogil functions.

Original text: Direct calls to BLAS routines are possible via interfaces defined in ``sklearn.utils._cython_blas``.
Atomic rule: Reach BLAS from Cython through sklearn.utils._cython_blas.
Section context: Stated as a possibility at the end of the performance list, with no alternative offered and no prohibition on other routes.
Notes: Trigger: Cython code calling BLAS.

Original text:
Since scikit-learn can be built without OpenMP, it's necessary to protect each

Section context: 'The `_openmp_helpers` module ... provides protected versions of the OpenMP routines.'
Notes: Trigger: Cython code calling OpenMP.

To use OpenMP routines, they
must be ``cimported`` from this module and not from the OpenMP library directly:
Atomic rule: cimport OpenMP routines from sklearn.utils._openmp_helpers, not from the OpenMP library.
Section context: Worked as `from sklearn.utils._openmp_helpers cimport omp_get_max_threads`. 'The parallel loop, `prange`, is already protected by cython and can be used directly from `cython.parallel`.'
Notes: Trigger: Cython code calling OpenMP routines other than prange.

Original text:
Cython code requires to use explicit types. This is one of the reasons you get a
performance boost.
Atomic rule: Declare explicit types in Cython code.
Section context: 'In order to avoid code duplication, we have a central place for the most used types in `sklearn/utils/_typedefs.pxd`.'
Notes: Trigger: Cython code.

Ideally you start by having a look there and `cimport` types you need, for example

    from sklearn.utils._typedefs cimport float32, float64
Atomic rule: cimport shared types from sklearn.utils._typedefs rather than redefining them.
Section context: 'Ideally'. The rationale given is avoiding code duplication; contributing.html notes 'scikit-learn codebase has a lot of non-unified (fused) types (re)definitions' with ongoing work to unify them.
Notes: Trigger: Cython code needing numeric types.

Original text:
To support callbacks, an estimator must inherit from the :class:`~CallbackSupportMixin`
class, which exposes the following methods:
Atomic rule: Inherit from CallbackSupportMixin to give an estimator callback support.
Section context: The page opens: 'Adding callback support in an estimator boils down to enabling the registration of callbacks, expressing fit as a tree of tasks, and invoking the callbacks at the beginning and end of each of these tasks.'
Notes: Trigger: contributions adding callback support to an estimator.

Original text:
:meth:`~CallbackSupportMixin._init_callback_context`, which should be called at the
  beginning of fit to create the root :class:`~CallbackContext`, corresponding to the
  task that represents the entire execution of `fit`.
Atomic rule: Call _init_callback_context at the start of fit to create the root callback context.
Section context: 'While the leading underscore signals that _init_callback_context is intended for internal use ... it is made available to developers building third-party estimators and should be considered part of the public API contract.'
Notes: Trigger: estimators supporting callbacks. An exact call at an exact point.

Original text:
For third-party estimators implementing callback support, the `fit` method should be
decorated with the :func:`~with_callbacks` decorator. This decorator guarantees that the
callbacks are torn down after `fit` finishes, even if it exits on an error.
Atomic rule: Decorate a third-party callback-supporting estimator's fit with with_callbacks.
Section context: 'For scikit-learn's built-in estimators, the :func:`~sklearn.base._fit_context` decorator already takes care of the callbacks teardown, thus :func:`~with_callbacks` should not be used.'
Notes: Trigger: third-party estimators only; inside scikit-learn the decorator is forbidden.

Original text:
For scikit-learn's built-in estimators, the :func:`~sklearn.base._fit_context` decorator
already takes care of the callbacks teardown, thus :func:`~with_callbacks` should not be
used.
Atomic rule: Do not use with_callbacks on a built-in scikit-learn estimator.
Section context: The complement of the third-party rule in the same paragraph; _fit_context already performs the teardown, so the decorator would double it.
Notes: Trigger: callback support added to an in-tree estimator.

Original text:
To be compatible with scikit-learn estimators, :term:`callbacks` must implement the
:class:`FitCallback` `protocol
Atomic rule: Implement the full FitCallback protocol on a callback.
Section context: The protocol is given in full: setup, on_fit_task_begin, on_fit_task_end and teardown, with the return type of each.
Notes: Trigger: contributions adding a callback. One conformance obligation covering the four hooks.

Original text:
In concrete implementations of callbacks, only the optional keyword-only arguments
  actually used by the hook should be explicitly declared in the hook signature.
Atomic rule: Declare only the optional hook arguments the callback actually uses.
Section context: 'The presence of an argument in the signature signals that the hook requires that argument, which allows the callback framework to avoid computing values that are not used by any registered callback.'
Notes: Trigger: callback hook implementations.

Original text:
These arguments must be defined as **keyword only**. If the kwargs are not keyword
      only, the values will not be provided to the hooks.
Atomic rule: Define a hook's optional arguments as keyword-only.
Section context: Given in a warning admonition with the failure mode attached: the values are silently not provided.
Notes: Trigger: callback hook implementations. Readable from the signature.

Original text:
Thus the
  implementation of the hooks should not expect to always receive a value for each of
  them and adapt their behavior accordingly.
Atomic rule: Handle a hook argument being absent rather than assuming it is always provided.
Section context: 'Even if requested, the optional arguments might or might not be provided by the estimator, depending on its ability to produce them at this task.'
Notes: Trigger: callback hook implementations.

Original text:
Callbacks should not rely on it to :term:`predict`, :term:`transform`, etc ... but
    rather use the `fitted_estimator` when available.
Atomic rule: Do not call predict or transform on the estimator a hook receives; use fitted_estimator.
Section context: 'The estimator instance received by the hooks ... is in the same state as it was when calling the hook during `fit`. Therefore it is not expected to be fully fitted (except for the teardown hook).'
Notes: Trigger: callback hook implementations.

Original text:
:term:`Auto-propagated <auto-propagated>` callbacks, i.e. callbacks that are expected to
be propagated from meta-estimators to their sub-estimators, must implement the
:class:`~AutoPropagatedCallback` protocol, an extension of the :class:`~FitCallback`
protocol:
Atomic rule: Implement the AutoPropagatedCallback protocol on a callback meant to propagate to sub-estimators.
Section context: The extension is one member, `max_propagation_depth`, whose semantics for 0 and None are given in the next paragraph.
Notes: Trigger: callbacks intended to propagate into meta-estimators.

Original text:
Therefore, `setup` / `teardown` should
not reset the state of the callback, and `on_fit_task_begin` / `on_fit_task_end` should
accumulate data across all fits.
Atomic rule: Do not reset callback state in setup or teardown; accumulate across fits.
Section context: 'Indeed resetting state in `setup` / `teardown` would drop information collected from previous or concurrent fits', because the estimator may be cloned and fitted many times inside a meta-estimator.
Notes: Trigger: callback implementations holding state.

Original text:

explicit seeding of their own independent RNG instances instead of relying on
the numpy or Python standard library RNG singletons to make sure that test
results are independent of the test execution order.
Atomic rule: Seed each test's own RNG instance instead of relying on the global RNG singletons.
Section context: 'However some tests might forget to use explicit seeding and this variable is a way to control the initial state of the aforementioned singletons.'
Notes: Trigger: tests using randomness. The develop.html random-number rules state the same for library code.

Original text:
All tests that use this fixture accept the contract that they should
deterministically pass for any seed value from 0 to 99 included.
Atomic rule: Make a test using the global_random_seed fixture pass for every seed from 0 to 99.
Section context: 'The range of admissible seed values is limited to [0, 99] because it is often not possible to write a test that can work for any possible seed and we want to avoid having tests that randomly fail on the CI.'
Notes: Trigger: tests using the global_random_seed fixture. An exact, closed seed range.

Original text:
When writing a new test function that uses this fixture, please use the
following command to make sure that it passes deterministically for all
admissible seeds on your local machine:

.. prompt:: bash $

    SKLEARN_TESTS_GLOBAL_RANDOM_SEED="all" pytest -v -k test_your_test_name
Atomic rule: Run a new global_random_seed test with SKLEARN_TESTS_GLOBAL_RANDOM_SEED="all" before submitting.
Section context: 'This can take a long time: only use for individual tests, not the full test suite!'
Notes: Trigger: newly written tests using the fixture. An exact invocation.

the CI config of pull-requests to make sure that our friendly contributors are
not the first people to encounter a seed-sensitivity regression in a test
unrelated to the changes of their own PR.
Atomic rule: Do not set SKLEARN_TESTS_GLOBAL_RANDOM_SEED in the pull-request CI configuration.
Section context: 'Only the scikit-learn maintainers who watch the results of the nightly builds are expected to be annoyed by this.'
Notes: Governs the CI configuration files, and only where a PR touches them.

Original text:
These are tools used to check and validate input.  When you write a function
which accepts arrays, matrices, or sparse matrices as arguments, the following
should be used when applicable.
Atomic rule: Use the sklearn.utils validation tools in functions accepting arrays or sparse matrices.
Section context: Followed by the catalogue of helpers (assert_all_finite, as_float_array, check_array, check_X_y, indexable, check_memory). develop.html states the same instruction as 'When applicable, use the validation tools and scripts in the sklearn.utils module.'
Notes: 'When applicable' leaves the trigger to the author's reading of the function.

Original text:
If your code relies on a random number generator, it should never use
functions like ``numpy.random.random`` or ``numpy.random.normal``.  This
approach can lead to repeatability issues in unit tests.
Atomic rule: Never call numpy.random.random or numpy.random.normal in library code.
Section context: develop.html states the same prohibition in its Random Numbers section as 'do not use ``numpy.random.random()`` or similar routines'; this page phrases it as 'should never'.
Notes: Same prohibition as the develop.html random-number rule, on a second page.

Instead, a
``numpy.random.RandomState`` object should be used, which is built from
a ``random_state`` argument passed to the class or function.
Atomic rule: Build a RandomState from a random_state argument passed to the class or function.

Notes: Same construction rule as develop.html's Random Numbers section.

Original text:
When implementing a new algorithm is thus recommended to **start
implementing it in Python using Numpy and Scipy** by taking care of avoiding
looping code using the vectorized idioms of those libraries.
Atomic rule: Implement a new algorithm in NumPy and SciPy before reaching for a compiled language.
Section context: 'In general, the scikit-learn project emphasizes the **readability** of the source code'. The numbered strategy that follows is only reached 'Sometimes however an algorithm cannot be expressed efficiently in simple vectorized Numpy code'.
Notes: Trigger: new algorithm implementations.

Original text:
In practice
this means trying to **replace any nested for loops by calls to equivalent
Numpy array methods**.
Atomic rule: Replace nested Python for loops with vectorized NumPy calls.
Section context: 'The goal is to avoid the CPU wasting time in the Python interpreter rather than crunching numbers to fit your statistical model.'
Notes: Trigger: numerical code. 'Trying to' hedges an otherwise exact instruction.

Original text:
**Profile** the Python implementation to find the main bottleneck and
   isolate it in a **dedicated module level function**. This function
   will be reimplemented as a compiled extension module.
Atomic rule: Isolate the profiled bottleneck in a dedicated module-level function before compiling it.
Section context: Step 1 of the four-step strategy for code that cannot be vectorized; steps 2 and 3 choose between wrapping an existing C/C++ library and writing Cython.
Notes: Trigger: contributions adding a compiled extension.

Original text:
If there exists a well maintained BSD or MIT **C/C++** implementation
   of the same algorithm that is not too big, you can write a
   **Cython wrapper** for it and include a copy of the source code
   of the library in the scikit-learn source tree
Atomic rule: Wrap an existing permissively licensed C/C++ implementation rather than rewriting it.
Section context: 'this strategy is used for the classes :class:`svm.LinearSVC`, :class:`svm.SVC` and :class:`linear_model.LogisticRegression` (wrappers for liblinear and libsvm)'. The licence condition is exact; 'not too big' is not.
Notes: Trigger: contributions adding a compiled implementation.

**Move the Python version of the function in the tests** and use
   it to check that the results of the compiled extension are consistent
   with the gold standard, easy to debug Python version.
Atomic rule: Keep the Python version of a compiled function in the tests as the reference implementation.
Section context: Step 4 of the strategy: the Python version becomes the gold standard the compiled extension is asserted against.
Notes: Trigger: contributions replacing a Python function with a compiled extension.

Original text:
Once the code is optimized (not simple bottleneck spottable by
   profiling), check whether it is possible to have **coarse grained
   parallelism** that is amenable to **multi-processing** by using the
   ``joblib.Parallel`` class.
Atomic rule: Consider coarse-grained joblib.Parallel parallelism once the hot path is optimized.
Section context: Step 5, conditioned on there being no simple bottleneck left; the class to use is named exactly.
Notes: Trigger: optimized numerical code.
